Sparse attention pattern ossification under extended context fine-tuning asks whether the dynamic, context-sensitive routing that transformer attention heads develop during pretraining gets "frozen" into rigid, document-structure-dependent habits when models are fine-tuned on long-context corpora — and whether this freezing degrades generalization when the model encounters document structures dissimilar from those seen during fine-tuning. The key concepts are: (1) head specialization, whereby individual attention heads develop interpretable functional roles (syntactic, positional, coreference, etc.) during pretraining; (2) pattern ossification, the hypothesis that extended fine-tuning on long documents causes these heads to overfit their attention distributions to structural regularities specific to the training distribution (e.g., legal docs with consistent section headers, or code with rigid scoping); and (3) structural heterogeneity, the degree to which target-domain documents violate the positional and syntactic assumptions baked into the fine-tuned patterns. The expert worry — invisible to beginners — is not that attention heads become specialized (that's expected and healthy), but that the gradient signal during long-context fine-tuning is dominated by position-proximal token pairs, causing heads to reinforce proximity-based attention biases rather than maintaining the flexible long-range retrieval capacity that motivated extended context training in the first place. Concretely, a model fine-tuned on long legal contracts may learn to hard-route attention toward clause-boundary tokens, then catastrophically misroute on biomedical literature where semantic dependencies span subsection boundaries in structurally incompatible ways — while standard perplexity metrics on held-out legal data show no degradation, masking the failure entirely.

The mechanistic pathway runs through gradient magnitude asymmetry: during long-context fine-tuning, the cross-entropy loss on locally-predictable tokens (function words, formulaic clause continuations, syntactically forced completions) is low but their gradients w.r.t. attention weights are non-zero and structurally biased — they systematically reward heads that attend to the immediately preceding 50–200 tokens where the predictive signal lives, while the rare long-range retrieval events (a pronoun resolving to an antecedent 8,000 tokens back) contribute high per-token loss but are diluted in the batch average because they occur infrequently relative to the sea of local predictions. Olsson et al. The loss-dominance hypothesis is substantially correct: Press et al.'s ALiBi work and subsequent RoPE ablations (Su et al., 2023) both show that models assign disproportionate probability mass to tokens within the local window even at 32K+ context lengths, meaning the gradient signal is positionally skewed by construction under standard causal LM loss. Concretely, a head that was retrieving a definition from position 1,200 while generating at position 9,400 will see its Q-K alignment gradually corrupted if every fine-tuning step also asks it to predict "the" after "pursuant to" using only local context — the same weight matrix cannot simultaneously maintain both geometric configurations under SGD without explicit regularization. This is compounded by attention entropy collapse: fine-tuning encourages heads to sharpen their distributions (lower entropy = lower loss variance), and sharpening on local tokens is the path of least resistance because local token co-occurrence statistics are dense and reliable, whereas long-range dependencies require maintaining diffuse, high-entropy attention over candidate positions until late in the forward pass. The dependency on easy-token loss domination is not just quantitative but qualitative: if you up-weight long-range dependency tokens (e.g., via retrieval-targeted loss masking as explored in LongLoRA, Chen et al., 2023), ossification slows measurably, confirming that the standard flat loss weighting is the proximate cause rather than fine-tuning per se.

Freezing Q and K projections during fine-tuning does substantially preserve attention routing geometry — empirical support comes from Lora-FA (Zhang et al., 2023), which freezes A (the down-projection) in LoRA adapters and finds that routing stability is maintained while content adaptation proceeds through the B matrix, suggesting the Q/K subspace is the locus of structural routing rather than semantic content. The functional dissociation is mechanistically clean in theory: Q and K weights determine which positions attend to which (the routing graph), while V and output projections determine what information is extracted and mixed once routing is fixed — so freezing Q/K should, in principle, lock the attention topology while allowing the model to learn new content transformations appropriate to the long-context fine-tuning domain. However, the picture is dirtier in practice because Q and K are not routing-only: the same Q/K dot-product geometry encodes both positional preference (local vs. long-range) and semantic key-matching (attending to tokens with specific content features), and these two functions are entangled in the same weight matrices — freezing Q/K to preserve long-range routing simultaneously freezes the semantic query formation, which can prevent the model from learning domain-appropriate retrieval cues (e.g., learning that in biomedical text, method section headers are reliable retrieval anchors). Voita et al. (2019) showed in their head pruning analysis that heads divide into "positional," "syntactic," and "rare word" specialists, but this specialization is distributed across Q, K, and V jointly — a positional head's routing behavior depends on V outputting position-correlated content that reinforces the Q/K routing signal in subsequent layers, so clean separation of routing and content into Q/K vs. V/O is an approximation that breaks at depth. The deeper implication is that "structural routing" is not purely a Q/K property but an emergent circuit property spanning Q, K, V, and the MLP layers that post-process attention output — what Anthropic's transformer circuits work calls a "virtual weight" composed across multiple linear maps. Practically, partial freezing strategies (freeze Q/K, train V/O) reduce ossification relative to full fine-tuning but don't eliminate it, because gradient pressure on V/O still reshapes what content gets routed even when the routing topology is fixed — the model learns to make locally-attended tokens more predictively useful, indirectly reinforcing proximity bias in the effective information flow even without touching Q/K.

Residual stream intervention is mechanistically more principled because it targets the information bottleneck rather than individual parameter groups — if you constrain how much the attention sublayer can shift the residual stream during fine-tuning (e.g., via a per-layer scalar gate or an L2 penalty on the attention output delta ∥Attn(x) - Attn₀(x)∥), you directly limit ossification of the routing circuit without freezing the weights that compute it, preserving the geometric relationships between Q, K, and V while allowing gradual adaptation. The closest empirical instantiation is BitFit (Zaken et al., 2022) and its successors, which show that fine-tuning only bias terms — which additively shift the residual stream at specific points — achieves competitive adaptation with far less disruption to pretrained weight geometry, implying that residual-level interventions carry disproportionate adaptive leverage relative to their parameter count. More directly, the NTK-aware scaling work on RoPE (Liu et al., 2023, "Scaling Laws of RoPE-based Extrapolation") demonstrates that attention sublayer contributions to the residual become pathologically large at extended context positions during naive fine-tuning, and that scaling down positional encoding magnitudes to rebalance residual contributions recovers long-range retrieval — this is effectively a residual-stream-level regularization achieving exactly the preservation goal. The limitation of this approach is that MLP sublayers in middle-to-late layers function as key-value memories (Geva et al., 2021) storing factual associations that may need substantial updating during domain fine-tuning, so a uniform attention/MLP residual regularization will either under-adapt the MLP memories or over-constrain the attention routing depending on the regularization strength chosen — the two sublayer types have asymmetric adaptation requirements that a single residual-level knob cannot simultaneously satisfy. A more principled decomposition would require layer-type-specific and depth-specific regularization schedules, since early attention layers primarily handle local syntactic routing (low ossification risk, high adaptation cost if frozen), middle layers handle the long-range retrieval circuits most vulnerable to ossification, and late layers perform output formatting that is both safe to adapt and necessary for domain transfer. The open engineering question is whether the residual stream delta penalty can be made adaptive per head rather than per layer — penalizing only heads whose attention entropy drops below a threshold during fine-tuning — which would selectively protect the high-entropy long-range retrieval heads while allowing low-entropy local heads to adapt freely, but no published system has implemented this with rigorous ablation as of mid-2025.

The propagation direction question is empirically resolvable and the answer appears to be both pathways operate but on different timescales: bottom-up corruption from positional encoding distortion manifests within the first few hundred gradient steps (because RoPE/ALiBi parameters influence every layer's Q/K dot products simultaneously), while top-down pressure from output distribution reshaping accumulates more slowly through the chain rule as late-layer loss gradients backpropagate through the residual stream. Layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD), canonically applied in ULMFiT (Howard & Ruder, 2018) and later in BERT fine-tuning (Sun et al., 2019 "How to Fine-Tune BERT"), was designed to address top-down gradient dominance by assigning lower learning rates to early layers — but this was motivated by catastrophic forgetting of syntactic features, not long-range retrieval preservation, and the schedules used (typically 0.9× decay per layer downward) were calibrated for short-context tasks where bottom-up positional corruption is not a failure mode. When applied to long-context fine-tuning, LLRD creates a pathological asymmetry: middle layers receive intermediate learning rates that are high enough to be corrupted by top-down output pressure but too low to resist bottom-up positional signal distortion propagating upward from early layers — neither corruption pathway is blocked, and the middle-layer retrieval circuits sit in the worst position. Reverse-layer update ordering (updating later layers first, then earlier layers within each step) has been explored in the context of curriculum learning for transformers (Press et al., 2022 "Measuring and Improving Consistency in Pretrained Language Models") and theoretically should allow late layers to stabilize their output targets before early layers adapt their representations, reducing top-down gradient pressure — but in practice the within-step sequential update is dominated by the global learning rate and the effect is modest unless combined with explicit gradient stopping between layer groups. The cleanest experimental evidence for propagation directionality comes from probing studies during fine-tuning: Merchant et al. (2020) showed that syntactic structure representations in middle BERT layers degrade before surface-level output statistics change, suggesting bottom-up corruption precedes top-down pressure for structural (routing-relevant) representations — which implies that for ossification specifically, positional encoding corruption is the earlier and more tractable intervention point. The practical implication is that a fine-tuning schedule that freezes the embedding and first 2–3 layers for the initial N steps (blocking bottom-up corruption) before unfreezing with low learning rates, combined with LLRD protecting middle layers from top-down pressure in later steps, should outperform either intervention alone — but this two-phase approach has not been systematically evaluated for long-range retrieval preservation as a distinct objective.

The injection site difference is mechanistically decisive for ossification vulnerability: RoPE applies positional bias multiplicatively inside the Q/K dot product via rotation matrices, meaning positional and semantic components of the attention score are entangled at the point of computation and cannot be independently regularized — any fine-tuning gradient that adjusts Q or K weights to improve next-token prediction simultaneously corrupts the rotational geometry encoding relative position, making RoPE-based models particularly vulnerable to bottom-up ossification when fine-tuned on documents with position statistics different from pretraining. ALiBi injects positional bias additively as a fixed scalar penalty to attention logits after the Q/K dot product, which means the semantic routing computed by Q and K is structurally decoupled from positional preference — fine-tuning gradients on Q/K weights update semantic key-matching without directly perturbing the positional decay schedule, giving ALiBi an architectural advantage in preserving long-range retrieval geometry during fine-tuning, consistent with Press et al.'s (2022) finding that ALiBi extrapolates to longer contexts than RoPE without fine-tuning at all. Learned absolute positional embeddings (as in original GPT-2/GPT-3) are the most vulnerable by a different mechanism: the position embeddings are trainable parameters in the residual stream that receive direct gradient updates during fine-tuning, and on long-context corpora where positions 0–512 are vastly overrepresented in locally-predictable tokens, the embeddings for early positions are pulled toward proximity-rewarding representations while embeddings for positions >4K may receive insufficient gradient signal to maintain their pretraining geometry — a form of positional embedding collapse documented in the context length generalization failures of early GPT-3 fine-tunes. The vulnerability ordering under extended context fine-tuning is approximately: learned absolute > RoPE > ALiBi, but this ranking interacts critically with the fine-tuning data's position distribution — RoPE's vulnerability is specifically acute when the fine-tuning corpus has document length distributions that concentrate tokens in the 0–2K range (legal paragraph-chunked data, for instance), because the high-frequency rotation angles used for short positions get reinforced while long-distance rotation angles decay toward noise. Empirical confirmation comes from LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023), which found that Llama-2 (RoPE-based) required explicit shifted sparse attention patterns during fine-tuning to prevent retrieval degradation at 32K — a workaround for RoPE's entanglement problem that would be unnecessary under ALiBi's additive scheme. The underappreciated implication is that RoPE's NTK-aware interpolation (bloc97, 2023; later formalized by Liu et al.) partially mitigates ossification by rescaling rotation frequencies to spread positional signal across the full target context length before fine-tuning, effectively pre-corrupting the short-range rotation geometry to prevent it from dominating gradients — a counterintuitive fix that works by making all positions equally unfamiliar rather than preserving any particular geometric structure.

ALiBi's fixed positional schedule provides zero protection against semantic ossification because the Q/K weights that compute content-based key matching are fully trainable and receive the same domain-skewed gradient signal as in any other architecture — the additive positional term is downstream of Q/K computation, so fine-tuning on legal contracts will still drive Q matrices to form queries that pattern-match on "whereas," "hereinafter," and clause-boundary tokens regardless of the positional scheme in use. Semantic ossification is mechanistically distinct: rather than heads learning to prefer nearby positions, they learn to prefer domain-specific token identities as retrieval anchors, which means the failure manifests as attention routing that works correctly within the fine-tuning domain's vocabulary distribution but catastrophically misfires when those lexical anchors are absent — a biomedical document with no clause boundaries offers no purchase for legal-ossified attention heads, even at short ranges where positional bias is irrelevant. The argument that semantic ossification is the more dangerous long-term failure mode is strong for heterogeneous document generalization: positional ossification at least degrades gracefully and predictably (performance drops monotonically with distance from the fine-tuning length distribution), whereas semantic ossification produces non-monotonic, structurally unpredictable failures where a model may correctly retrieve information at 16K tokens in legal text but fail at 512 tokens in a biomedical abstract because the key tokens it learned to query for simply don't exist. Evidence for the severity of semantic ossification comes obliquely from domain transfer studies: Gururangan et al. (2020) "Don't Stop Pretraining" showed that domain-adaptive pretraining produces representations that are less transferable across domains than the original pretrained model despite higher in-domain performance, which is precisely the signature of semantic ossification — the model's internal retrieval keys have been sharpened for one domain's lexical statistics at the cost of cross-domain generalization. The interaction between positional and semantic ossification is also underappreciated: in RoPE models, the two pathways co-corrupt because the rotation geometry encodes both relative distance and, implicitly, token identity correlations (tokens that co-occur at specific relative distances get their rotational representations entangled), so semantic and positional ossification reinforce each other in a way that ALiBi models partially escape by keeping the positional channel clean. The expert concern is that standard evaluation protocols are blind to semantic ossification almost by design: benchmarks like SCROLLS, QuALITY, and LongBench are constructed within relatively homogeneous document distributions, so a model with severely ossified Q/K weights tuned to that distribution will score well while harboring a retrieval architecture that is brittle to any structural novelty — the evaluation corpus and the ossification corpus are drawn from the same distribution, guaranteeing the failure is invisible until deployment on heterogeneous real-world documents.

Quantifying semantic ossification via key distribution divergence is tractable and the right measurement target: for each attention head, you collect the empirical distribution of activated key vectors (the K-projection outputs that receive non-negligible attention weight) across a held-out in-domain corpus and a structurally heterogeneous out-of-domain corpus, then measure the Jensen-Shannon divergence between these distributions in the head's key subspace — heads with high JSD are routing to domain-specific anchors, heads with low JSD are generalizing. The methodological precedent exists in attention head analysis tooling: Clark et al. (2019) "What Does BERT Look At?" characterized head behavior by aggregating attention weight distributions across token types, and the same aggregation logic applies here with the modification that you're measuring key-space activation patterns rather than attention weight targets, which is more informative because it captures what the head is looking for rather than what it finds. A practical ossification audit protocol would proceed in four steps: (1) extract K-projection activations for all heads across 500–1000 documents each from in-domain and out-of-domain corpora; (2) project to the top-50 PCA dimensions of the in-domain key distribution to get a tractable subspace; (3) compute JSD or MMD (maximum mean discrepancy) between in-domain and out-of-domain key activation clouds per head; (4) flag heads in the top quartile of divergence as ossification candidates, then verify by ablating those heads and measuring task performance degradation on out-of-domain retrieval tasks — heads whose ablation improves out-of-domain performance are confirmed semantic ossification sites. The audit should also include an entropy delta metric: comparing each head's attention entropy on in-domain versus out-of-domain documents identifies heads that are confidently routing on in-domain text but collapsing to near-uniform or near-degenerate distributions on out-of-domain text, which is the behavioral signature of a head whose learned anchors are absent in the new domain. Operationally, this protocol is feasible with existing interpretability infrastructure — TransformerLens (Nanda et al.) and BertViz both expose per-head K activations and attention patterns at inference time without architectural modification, meaning the audit can be run on any deployed model without retraining. The critical calibration challenge is choosing the out-of-domain corpus to be structurally maximal rather than merely topically different: a legal model audited against financial documents may show low JSD because both domains share clause-boundary anchor tokens, masking ossification that would be revealed by biomedical or conversational out-of-domain text — the audit is only as sensitive as the structural diversity of the contrast corpus.
